units.teachingGoal: Give the reader a compelling reason to understand AI and the first complete map she can use immediately.
questionsAnswered: Why does understanding AI matter in my ordinary decisions and work?
What does the label AI tell me, and what does it leave unanswered?
What first questions make an AI claim more concrete?

sections.title: Why this matters before the next AI decision
sections.teachingGoal: Make the personal and practical value of understanding AI felt before technical explanation begins.
relationshipsAdded: Vague AI claims can lead to different human consequences depending on what the system actually does.
questionsAnswered: Why should I care what sits behind an AI claim?
sections.learnerEvidence: EXPLAIN_IT: name one decision that changes when the underlying AI system changes.

sections.title: The first map of an AI system
sections.teachingGoal: Establish the input to system to output to consequence path used throughout the book.
relationshipsAdded: An AI system processes an input into an output that may influence a later action or decision.
questionsAnswered: What is the shortest useful description of an AI system?
What can happen after an AI output is produced?
sections.learnerEvidence: DRAW_IT: reproduce input to system to output to consequence with directional arrows.

sections.title: Three questions that replace the vague label
sections.teachingGoal: Give the reader an immediate practical method for turning an AI label into an examinable system.
relationshipsAdded: Asking what a system does, what it uses and what follows its output reveals different design and risk choices.
questionsAnswered: What should I ask when someone says a product uses AI?
sections.learnerEvidence: USE_IT: apply the three questions to an unfamiliar workplace AI proposal.

units.teachingGoal: Orient the reader to the major kinds and capability claims without presenting unlike labels as one flat taxonomy.
questionsAnswered: Why do very different products all count as AI?
What do predictive, generative, multimodal and agentic describe?
What are AGI and ASI, and do they exist today?

sections.title: AI is an umbrella, not one machine
sections.teachingGoal: Show that AI names a broad field of systems rather than one product, model or behaviour.
relationshipsAdded: Many systems fit beneath AI while performing different tasks with different components.
questionsAnswered: Why can two very different systems both be AI?
sections.learnerEvidence: EXPLAIN_IT: compare two familiar AI systems without claiming they work identically.

sections.title: Systems that recognise, predict, rank and recommend
sections.teachingGoal: Make common non-generative AI tasks visible in familiar products.
relationshipsAdded: Recognition and prediction can feed ranking, and ranking can feed a recommendation shown by a product.
questionsAnswered: What is the difference between recognising, predicting, ranking and recommending?
Where do I encounter them?
sections.learnerEvidence: USE_IT: identify the task performed by a spam filter and a streaming recommendation.

sections.title: Generative and multimodal AI
sections.teachingGoal: Explain content generation and distinguish it from the kinds of information a system can receive and produce.
relationshipsAdded: Generative describes producing new content, while multimodal describes handling more than one kind of input or output.
questionsAnswered: What makes a system generative?
What makes a system multimodal?
Can one system be both?
sections.learnerEvidence: EXPLAIN_IT: classify a text-and-image assistant using both labels without treating them as competitors.

sections.title: Agentic and embodied systems
sections.teachingGoal: Introduce continued multi-step operation and physical-world interaction without yet teaching the full implementation.
relationshipsAdded: Agentic describes continued operation toward a goal; embodied describes interaction through a physical body or environment; either may use generative components.
questionsAnswered: What does agentic describe?
What does embodied describe?
Do either imply consciousness or correctness?
sections.learnerEvidence: USE_IT: distinguish a chatbot, a tool-using assistant and a warehouse robot.

sections.title: AGI and ASI
sections.teachingGoal: Place disputed and hypothetical general-intelligence claims beside present systems without implying an inevitable progression.
relationshipsAdded: AGI concerns disputed breadth and transfer across unfamiliar intellectual tasks, while ASI is a hypothetical claim of capability beyond humans across broad domains.
questionsAnswered: What do AGI and ASI mean?
Do they exist today?
Why do credible definitions and forecasts disagree?
sections.learnerEvidence: EXPLAIN_IT: distinguish a capable current general-purpose product from the book's ruled AGI and ASI boundaries.

sections.title: How the labels overlap
sections.teachingGoal: Help the reader combine task, modality, operating pattern and breadth labels without building a false flat taxonomy.
relationshipsAdded: A single product may truthfully receive several labels because the labels answer different questions about its behaviour or claimed breadth.
questionsAnswered: How can several AI labels be true at once?
Which labels should not be treated as peers?
sections.learnerEvidence: DRAW_IT: place task, modality, operating pattern and breadth on separate branches around one product.

units.teachingGoal: Separate the visible product from the model and surrounding technical and human components.
questionsAnswered: What is an AI model?
What else makes an AI product work?
Why can the same model behave differently in different products?

sections.title: The product you can see
sections.teachingGoal: Separate the interface and product experience from the complete underlying system.
relationshipsAdded: The interface is the visible point of interaction with a larger AI product.
questionsAnswered: What is the difference between an interface and an AI product?
sections.learnerEvidence: DRAW_IT: place the interface as the visible edge of the larger product.

sections.title: The model inside the product
sections.teachingGoal: Define a model before discussing training and keep it distinct from product and company.
relationshipsAdded: A model is a trained component that maps inputs to outputs inside a wider product system.
questionsAnswered: What is an AI model?
Is a model the same as the product or company?
sections.learnerEvidence: EXPLAIN_IT: describe the model's job without calling it the whole application.

sections.title: Instructions, rules and orchestration
sections.teachingGoal: Show how surrounding software decides what information reaches the model and what happens to its output.
relationshipsAdded: Product software assembles instructions and inputs, invokes the model and governs possible downstream handling.
questionsAnswered: What does the software around a model do?
Why can product behaviour differ even when the underlying model is the same?
sections.learnerEvidence: USE_IT: identify one behaviour likely controlled by the product rather than the model alone.

sections.title: Information, memory and tools around the model
sections.teachingGoal: Orient the reader to optional supporting components before later chapters explain them fully.
relationshipsAdded: A product may supply retrieved information or memory to a model and may route model output to tools.
questionsAnswered: Which useful capabilities may sit outside the model?
sections.learnerEvidence: DRAW_IT: add retrieval memory and tools around rather than inside the model box.

sections.title: Computers, companies and people
sections.teachingGoal: Place physical infrastructure and human decisions into the system from the beginning.
relationshipsAdded: Hardware runs the model and product, while organisations and people choose objectives, access, permissions and use.
questionsAnswered: Where does an AI product physically run?
Which important choices remain human or institutional?
sections.learnerEvidence: EXPLAIN_IT: add one infrastructure choice and one human decision to the product map.

sections.title: How products assemble the parts
sections.teachingGoal: Introduce service boundaries, APIs and inference serving without assuming software-engineering knowledge.
relationshipsAdded: Interfaces and application services exchange structured requests with model and tool services across controlled boundaries.
questionsAnswered: How do separate software services cooperate to produce one AI product experience?
sections.learnerEvidence: DRAW_IT: expand the product box into interface application model and tool services.

units.teachingGoal: Explain how a model is built, adjusted and evaluated, then distinguish that process from using it on a new input.
questionsAnswered: How does machine learning differ from ordinary programmed rules?
What happens during training?
What are tokens, parameters, neural networks and transformers?
How are training, post-training, evaluation and inference different?

sections.title: From written rules to learned patterns
sections.teachingGoal: Introduce machine learning as pattern acquisition from examples rather than a complete list of hand-written rules.
relationshipsAdded: A learning algorithm uses examples and an objective to adjust a model rather than requiring a programmer to specify every mapping.
questionsAnswered: What is machine learning?
How is it different from writing every rule directly?
sections.learnerEvidence: EXPLAIN_IT: contrast a hand-written spam rule with a model trained on examples.

sections.title: Neural networks and deep learning
sections.teachingGoal: Place neural networks and deep learning inside machine learning without implying that all AI uses them.
relationshipsAdded: Deep learning uses neural networks with multiple learned layers and is one family within machine learning.
questionsAnswered: What is a neural network?
What makes deep learning deep?
Is all AI deep learning?
sections.learnerEvidence: DRAW_IT: place deep learning within neural networks within machine learning within AI.

sections.title: How language becomes model input
sections.teachingGoal: Make tokenisation and learned numeric representations understandable before transformer mechanics.
relationshipsAdded: Text is divided into tokens and represented numerically so a model can process learned relationships among them.
questionsAnswered: What is a token?
Why does a language model not receive words exactly as people see them?
What job does an embedding perform?
sections.learnerEvidence: EXPLAIN_IT: trace a short sentence from visible text to tokens to numeric representations.

sections.title: The training loop
sections.teachingGoal: Explain prediction, error measurement and repeated parameter adjustment as one causal loop.
relationshipsAdded: The training objective defines a measured error, and optimisation repeatedly adjusts parameters to reduce that error across examples.
questionsAnswered: What actually changes during training?
What tells the training process which direction is better?
sections.learnerEvidence: DRAW_IT: show example to prediction to error to parameter adjustment to next example.

sections.title: Transformers and attention
sections.teachingGoal: Explain the central relationship-tracking mechanism used by modern language models without treating it as human attention.
relationshipsAdded: A transformer processes token representations while attention mechanisms compute context-dependent relationships among positions.
questionsAnswered: What is a transformer?
What does attention do?
Why is it not the same as human attention or understanding?
sections.learnerEvidence: EXPLAIN_IT: describe how one token's useful representation can depend on surrounding tokens.

sections.title: Post-training and evaluation
sections.teachingGoal: Separate broad pattern learning from later behaviour shaping and from tests used to assess the resulting system.
relationshipsAdded: Post-training further shapes behaviour after broad training, while evaluation measures selected capabilities and failures without guaranteeing every real use.
questionsAnswered: What happens after initial training?
What can an evaluation show and what can it miss?
sections.learnerEvidence: USE_IT: distinguish a behaviour-shaping step from a test of the resulting behaviour.

sections.title: Using the trained model
sections.teachingGoal: Make inference distinct from training and prepare for the next chapter's current-information pathways.
relationshipsAdded: Inference applies a trained model to a current input; useful performance on appropriate new cases is generalisation, not fresh training during every request.
questionsAnswered: What is inference?
Why is adding information to a prompt not ordinarily the same as retraining the model?
What does generalisation mean?
sections.learnerEvidence: USE_IT: classify building a spam model and checking one new email as training or inference.

units.teachingGoal: Separate what the model learned during training from what the product supplies or stores for a current request.
questionsAnswered: What information can an AI product use right now?
How are context, retrieval and memory different?
Why might information visible to me still be absent from the model's current input?

sections.title: Patterns learned during training
sections.teachingGoal: Explain why a model's parameters are not a browsable database of its training material.
relationshipsAdded: Training changes parameters that encode learned patterns, but inference does not retrieve a neat source record from those parameters.
questionsAnswered: What does a trained model retain?
Why can it not reliably show the source of every learned pattern?
sections.learnerEvidence: EXPLAIN_IT: distinguish learned parameters from a searchable document store.

sections.title: Your prompt and the product's instructions
sections.teachingGoal: Show that user requests and product instructions jointly shape the current model input.
relationshipsAdded: The product assembles user content and other instructions into the current request under an instruction hierarchy.
questionsAnswered: What is a prompt?
Why is my prompt not necessarily the only instruction the product uses?
sections.learnerEvidence: USE_IT: improve one vague delegation using the canonical Spice Girls desired-result cue plus context constraints and output form.

sections.title: Context and the context window
sections.teachingGoal: Explain the current working material and its bounded capacity.
relationshipsAdded: The model produces a result from tokens present in its current context, whose capacity and product selection rules are bounded.
questionsAnswered: What is context?
What is a context window?
Why might earlier material be missing?
sections.learnerEvidence: DRAW_IT: place current instructions conversation and attachments inside a bounded context container.

sections.title: Retrieval and current sources
sections.teachingGoal: Explain how a product can find external material and supply selected results to the model.
relationshipsAdded: Retrieval finds candidate information, selection chooses what enters context and the model uses that supplied material to generate output.
questionsAnswered: How can an AI product use current documents?
What does retrieval-augmented generation add?
Where can retrieval fail?
sections.learnerEvidence: DRAW_IT: show query to retrieval to selected source to context to model output.

sections.title: Conversation history and product memory
sections.teachingGoal: Separate stored information, selected history and information actually placed in context.
relationshipsAdded: A product may store history or memory, then selectively retrieve some of it into a later context; stored does not automatically mean currently used.
questionsAnswered: How are chat history, memory and current context different?
Can something be stored but absent from the current answer?
sections.learnerEvidence: EXPLAIN_IT: distinguish visible stored retrievable and currently supplied information.

sections.title: Finding the missing information
sections.teachingGoal: Give the reader a practical diagnosis for answers that lack current or relevant information.
relationshipsAdded: An answer may fail because information was never learned, not stored, not retrieved, not selected into context or poorly used after arrival.
questionsAnswered: Where could relevant information have gone missing?
What is the smallest useful correction for each failure?
sections.learnerEvidence: USE_IT: diagnose an answer based on an obsolete workplace policy.

units.teachingGoal: Trace the boundary between model output and an action executed through connected software under permissions.
questionsAnswered: How does an AI product use a tool?
What is the difference between connection, permission and execution?
How can I tell whether an action actually happened?

sections.title: From model output to a tool request
sections.teachingGoal: Explain how a model can produce structured output that surrounding software interprets as a proposed tool use.
relationshipsAdded: A model generates a structured request, and product software decides whether and how to route it to a tool.
questionsAnswered: What does the model itself produce when a tool may be used?
sections.learnerEvidence: DRAW_IT: place a proposed tool request between model output and product execution.

sections.title: Connections and permissions
sections.teachingGoal: Keep technical availability separate from authorised scope.
relationshipsAdded: A connector makes a tool reachable, while permissions determine which operations and data are authorised.
questionsAnswered: Does connecting a tool give the AI permission to do everything in it?
Who sets the permission boundary?
sections.learnerEvidence: EXPLAIN_IT: distinguish a connected calendar from permission to create or delete events.

sections.title: Execution and returned observations
sections.teachingGoal: Follow an authorised request through tool execution and the information returned to the product.
relationshipsAdded: The tool executes an authorised operation and returns an observation that may enter the next model context.
questionsAnswered: What proves that a requested action actually happened?
How does the result return to the AI system?
sections.learnerEvidence: DRAW_IT: complete the loop from request to permission to execution to observation.

sections.title: Confirmation before consequences
sections.teachingGoal: Place a proportional human checkpoint before consequential or irreversible actions.
relationshipsAdded: The need for human confirmation increases with consequence uncertainty and irreversibility.
questionsAnswered: When should a person confirm an AI-proposed action?
Why is a drafted action not the same as an approved one?
sections.learnerEvidence: USE_IT: choose a checkpoint for searching flights holding a fare and purchasing a ticket.

sections.title: APIs, authentication and safe execution
sections.teachingGoal: Explain the technical controls beneath a governed tool connection.
relationshipsAdded: Authenticated APIs expose bounded operations, least privilege narrows authority and idempotent design reduces accidental duplicate actions.
questionsAnswered: How are identity and permission enforced technically?
How can a system reduce duplicate or unauthorised actions?
sections.learnerEvidence: EXPLAIN_IT: connect authentication permission and execution without treating them as synonyms.

units.teachingGoal: Distinguish fixed automation, governed workflows and agentic loops, including their control and failure implications.
questionsAnswered: What makes an AI system agentic?
How is an agent different from automation or a workflow?
Why can errors compound across steps?

sections.title: Automation and governed workflows
sections.teachingGoal: Establish fixed and predesigned multi-step baselines before introducing agent loops.
relationshipsAdded: Automation follows predetermined conditions, while a workflow coordinates known stages and checkpoints.
questionsAnswered: What is automation?
What makes a workflow more than one automatic step?
sections.learnerEvidence: USE_IT: classify a scheduled reminder and a fixed approval route.

sections.title: The agent loop
sections.teachingGoal: Explain continued goal-directed operation through repeated model tool and observation cycles.
relationshipsAdded: An agent loop uses a goal and state to select a next step, call a tool, observe the result and continue or stop.
questionsAnswered: What is the repeating mechanism inside an agentic system?
What information must persist between steps?
sections.learnerEvidence: DRAW_IT: reconstruct goal to next step to tool to observation to updated state to stop-or-continue.

sections.title: Planning, routing and changing course
sections.teachingGoal: Show several ways a system can choose subsequent steps without implying human-style intention.
relationshipsAdded: A system may select from predefined routes or generate intermediate steps and revise them after observations.
questionsAnswered: How can an agent choose what to do next?
Does planning imply consciousness or independent desire?
sections.learnerEvidence: EXPLAIN_IT: distinguish generated planning from human intention.

sections.title: Stopping, escalation and control
sections.teachingGoal: Make stopping conditions and human escalation essential components rather than emergency additions.
relationshipsAdded: The loop continues only within stopping escalation permission and budget boundaries established by the product and organisation.
questionsAnswered: What should make an agent stop?
When should it escalate to a person?
sections.learnerEvidence: USE_IT: set stopping and escalation rules for an invoice-investigation agent.

sections.title: Why small mistakes can become large ones
sections.teachingGoal: Connect multi-step operation to error accumulation and verification placement.
relationshipsAdded: A mistaken output can become later context or action, causing subsequent steps to build on the error.
questionsAnswered: Why is a five-step agent riskier than five independent suggestions?
Where should checks occur?
sections.learnerEvidence: DRAW_IT: show how one early error propagates through two later steps and where a checkpoint interrupts it.

units.teachingGoal: Give the reader a system-level failure map so that different problems receive different diagnoses and responses.
questionsAnswered: What is a hallucination?
How are unreliability, brittleness, bias, manipulation and misuse different?
How do I locate the failure before choosing a safeguard?

sections.title: Hallucinations and unsupported claims
sections.teachingGoal: Explain fluent unsupported output and the difference between presentation quality and evidential support.
relationshipsAdded: A model can generate a plausible claim without adequate support in current evidence or reliable learned patterns.
questionsAnswered: What is an AI hallucination?
Why can unsupported information sound authoritative?
What should I check?
sections.learnerEvidence: USE_IT: apply the canonical Burn Book authority-without-support mapping to a new AI claim and identify the needed source check.

sections.title: Unreliability and brittleness
sections.teachingGoal: Separate inconsistency across repeated or slightly changed cases from fabricated factual content.
relationshipsAdded: A system may perform well in tested conditions yet change sharply under small input or environment changes.
questionsAnswered: How can a correct-looking system still be unreliable?
What is brittleness?
sections.learnerEvidence: USE_IT: compare repeated outputs and one changed condition before drawing a reliability conclusion.

sections.title: Bias, fairness and unequal consequences
sections.teachingGoal: Connect data objectives design and institutional use to unequal outcomes without implying one universal fairness measure.
relationshipsAdded: Data representation objectives decision thresholds and deployment context can produce or amplify unequal outcomes.
questionsAnswered: Where can unfairness enter an AI system?
Why can reasonable fairness goals conflict?
sections.learnerEvidence: DRAW_IT: mark at least three places where unequal outcomes can enter or be amplified.

sections.title: Security, manipulation and adversarial use
sections.teachingGoal: Introduce deliberate attacks and unsafe authority as different from ordinary model error.
relationshipsAdded: Attackers may manipulate training data current context tool instructions or user behaviour to redirect system outcomes.
questionsAnswered: How is manipulation different from an accidental hallucination?
Which system layers can an attacker target?
sections.learnerEvidence: USE_IT: locate a malicious instruction hidden in retrieved content and choose the relevant control boundary.

sections.title: Tests, verification and evidence
sections.teachingGoal: Match evaluation and human checking to the specific claim task and consequence.
relationshipsAdded: A useful evaluation samples the failure that matters in the intended context, while verification checks consequential claims or actions against appropriate evidence.
questionsAnswered: What does it mean to verify an AI result?
Why is one benchmark or one request insufficient evidence?
sections.learnerEvidence: EXPLAIN_IT: match hallucination reliability fairness and tool execution to different checks.

sections.title: Diagnose the layer before fixing the problem
sections.teachingGoal: Unify the failure chapter into a practical system-diagnosis method.
relationshipsAdded: A visible bad result can originate in model data context retrieval tool workflow interface or institutional decision layers.
questionsAnswered: Where did this failure most likely originate?
What evidence would distinguish competing causes?
What is the smallest relevant response?
sections.learnerEvidence: USE_IT: diagnose four superficially similar policy-answer failures at different layers.

units.teachingGoal: Trace personal or organisational information through the complete product lifecycle and make product-specific privacy checks possible.
questionsAnswered: What can happen to information I provide?
What is the difference between current processing, storage, retrieval and possible training use?
Which product, account and workplace settings must I check?

sections.title: When information enters the product
sections.teachingGoal: Separate immediate request processing from later retention or reuse.
relationshipsAdded: Information enters a product for immediate processing under product organisational and legal choices.
questionsAnswered: What happens first when I provide information?
Who determines the initial processing purpose?
sections.learnerEvidence: DRAW_IT: begin a data path at collection and immediate processing.

sections.title: Storage, history and later retrieval
sections.teachingGoal: Connect privacy choices to the earlier distinction among stored retrievable and current information.
relationshipsAdded: Retained information may be available for history memory administration or retrieval depending on access and selection rules.
questionsAnswered: What is the difference between storage and current use?
What should deletion and retention controls tell me?
sections.learnerEvidence: EXPLAIN_IT: distinguish saved history from information placed in a later model context.

sections.title: Sharing and possible model-improvement use
sections.teachingGoal: Explain that provider sharing and training-use rules vary by product plan account and configuration.
relationshipsAdded: Retained product data may follow separate sharing or model-improvement paths only under the applicable terms settings and organisational configuration.
questionsAnswered: Does using an AI product automatically train the model on my information?
What determines whether data may be reused or shared?
sections.learnerEvidence: USE_IT: identify the exact policy and settings needed before making a training-use claim.

sections.title: Personal accounts and governed workplace systems
sections.teachingGoal: Make account and administrator configuration part of the privacy answer.
relationshipsAdded: The same provider may apply different data permissions retention and training-use rules across personal and workplace configurations.
questionsAnswered: Why can the same product name have different privacy answers?
What should I check in a workplace account?
sections.learnerEvidence: USE_IT: compare what must be verified before sharing a confidential meeting summary in two account types.

sections.title: A practical data-path decision
sections.teachingGoal: Turn the data lifecycle into a repeatable pre-use decision rather than a generic warning.
relationshipsAdded: A sharing decision should follow the actual collection processing retention access sharing and reuse path for the configured product.
questionsAnswered: Can I trace where this information may go?
Which unknown would stop me from sharing it?
sections.learnerEvidence: DRAW_IT_AND_USE_IT: map one confidential input and make a bounded share do-not-share decision.

units.teachingGoal: Extend the technical system into the wider AI ecosystem of organisations infrastructure work markets governance and public consequences.
questionsAnswered: Who builds, supplies, deploys, governs and is affected by AI systems?
How do chips, cloud services, data centres and energy connect to AI products?
How can I separate current evidence from forecasts about work, society and the future?

sections.title: Who builds and operates the AI ecosystem
sections.teachingGoal: Distinguish research labs model providers infrastructure providers application companies deployers users and affected people.
relationshipsAdded: Different organisations research models supply compute build products deploy systems and bear or distribute consequences.
questionsAnswered: Who performs which job in the AI ecosystem?
Why are model provider product provider and workplace deployer different?
sections.learnerEvidence: DRAW_IT: place the organisations behind one familiar AI product and label their distinct roles.

sections.title: Chips, cloud and data centres
sections.teachingGoal: Connect seemingly weightless AI use to physical computing and supply chains.
relationshipsAdded: Specialised chips run training and inference inside data centres exposed to products through infrastructure and cloud services.
questionsAnswered: What is a GPU doing in the AI ecosystem?
Where do training and inference physically happen?
sections.learnerEvidence: DRAW_IT: connect chip to server to data centre to model service to product.

sections.title: Open, open-weight and closed systems
sections.teachingGoal: Separate access to a product source code model weights and training information.
relationshipsAdded: Different release choices expose different combinations of code weights documentation data and usage rights.
questionsAnswered: What does open mean for an AI system?
Why is open-weight not automatically open source or unrestricted?
sections.learnerEvidence: EXPLAIN_IT: identify which asset and permission an openness claim actually covers.

sections.title: Tasks, jobs and organisational choices
sections.teachingGoal: Connect product deployment to task change accountability incentives and uneven effects without treating forecasts as facts.
relationshipsAdded: Organisations choose which tasks a system changes, who checks it, how gains are distributed and who bears failure.
questionsAnswered: How can AI change a task without replacing an entire job?
Which organisational decisions shape the outcome?
sections.learnerEvidence: USE_IT: analyse one workplace proposal by task change accountability and distribution of benefit and risk.

sections.title: Energy, water and material resources
sections.teachingGoal: Explain the physical resource pathway while preserving measurement uncertainty and scale differences.
relationshipsAdded: Training and serving models consume computing resources whose energy water and material effects depend on hardware location workload and accounting boundary.
questionsAnswered: Why does AI use physical resources?
Why can one environmental number be misleading without a boundary?
sections.learnerEvidence: EXPLAIN_IT: name the system boundary required before comparing two resource claims.

sections.title: Rules, evidence and possible futures
sections.teachingGoal: Give the reader a disciplined way to interpret regulation standards forecasts and AGI or labour scenarios.
relationshipsAdded: Governments standards bodies companies workers and communities shape system constraints, while evidence and forecasts carry different certainty.
questionsAnswered: Who governs AI and through which mechanisms?
How do I distinguish a current fact from a forecast or scenario?
What evidence would change the conclusion?
sections.learnerEvidence: USE_IT: label five ecosystem claims as fact company framing inference forecast disagreement or unknown.

units.teachingGoal: Prove that the learner owns one connected model she can reconstruct explain and use without reproducing the book's wording.
questionsAnswered: Can I explain how the complete AI ecosystem fits together?
Can I analyse an unfamiliar AI product or proposal?
Can I identify what is present absent unknown and consequential?

sections.title: Draw the complete system
sections.teachingGoal: Elicit the complete mental model from a blank page.
relationshipsAdded: The learner integrates technical and institutional layers into one directed map with optional components marked as optional.
questionsAnswered: Can I reconstruct the important components and relationships without the book in front of me?
sections.learnerEvidence: DRAW_IT: blank-page ecosystem reconstruction.

sections.title: Explain why the parts matter
sections.teachingGoal: Demonstrate causal understanding rather than diagram copying.
relationshipsAdded: The learner explains how changing information model product permission or institutional choices changes possible outcomes.
questionsAnswered: Can I explain how and why the parts work together in ordinary language?
sections.learnerEvidence: EXPLAIN_IT: teach one familiar AI product to another nontechnical person.

sections.title: Use the map on something new
sections.teachingGoal: Demonstrate transfer to an unfamiliar practical situation.
relationshipsAdded: The learner uses the model to identify present absent and unknown components, predict failures and choose useful questions or safeguards.
questionsAnswered: Can I analyse a new AI proposal and make a better practical judgment?
sections.learnerEvidence: USE_IT: unseen workplace AI proposal analysis.

units.teachingGoal: Support direct concept lookup without separating a term from its prerequisites mechanism and ecosystem relationship.
questionsAnswered: What does this term mean in plain language?
Where is it taught in the connected sequence?
What is it related to or commonly confused with?

sections.title: How to use the Concept Index
sections.teachingGoal: Explain lookup and route recovery without turning the book into a glossary.
relationshipsAdded: Every lookup term points to its first explanation, prerequisites and wider-system relationship.
questionsAnswered: How do I look up a term and return to the connected explanation?
sections.learnerEvidence: USE_IT: find a term from ordinary language and recover its chapter context.

sections.title: A to Z concept entries
sections.teachingGoal: Provide compact accurate retrieval while preserving distinctions and currentness.
relationshipsAdded: Each entry connects a plain meaning to one canonical anchor, adjacent distinction and ecosystem relationship.
questionsAnswered: What does this concept mean?
What should I not confuse it with?
Where does it belong in the AI ecosystem?
sections.learnerEvidence: EXPLAIN_IT: use one index entry to explain the concept's relationship rather than recite its definition.
